elements.text: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning  ·  DeepSeek-AI  ·  arXiv:2501.12948 (22 Jan 2025)
a visual breakdown, drawn in sketchboard
Page 1 of the paper — Ctrl+click to open the PDF

The question: can a large language model learn to reason — check its own work, back-track, think longer on hard problems — from reinforcement learning alone, with no human-written reasoning examples?

The answer: yes. DeepSeek-R1-Zero is DeepSeek-V3-Base trained with pure RL (GRPO + simple rule-based rewards). Its AIME 2024 score climbs from 15.6% to 71.0%, and long chains of thought, reflection and an “aha moment” emerge on their own.

R1-Zero is hard to read and mixes languages, so DeepSeek-R1 adds a little cold-start data and a 4-stage pipeline (SFT → RL → SFT → RL). It matches OpenAI-o1-1217 on reasoning benchmarks.

Finally, R1’s outputs (800k samples) are distilled into six small open models (1.5B–70B) that beat much bigger non-reasoning models.
R1 on Codeforces — beats 96.3% of humans
Bigger = better. All numbers are from the paper’s Tables 2, 4 and 5.

Post-training (everything after pre-training) has become a key part of building LLMs: it raises accuracy on reasoning tasks, aligns models with social values and adapts them to user preferences — for a small fraction of pre-training compute.

OpenAI’s o1 models were the first to use inference-time scaling: they get better by writing a longer chain of thought (CoT) before answering. How to achieve effective test-time scaling in the open was still an open question.

Can an LLM learn to reason with pure reinforcement learning — no supervised data at all?
Their bet: start from a strong base model (DeepSeek-V3-Base), use GRPO as the RL algorithm, and let reasoning self-evolve — just reward correct, well-formatted answers.

elements.text:
• RL straight on the base model, with no SFT warm-up, produces DeepSeek-R1-Zero. It learns self-verification, reflection and long CoTs.

• The first open research to validate that LLM reasoning can be incentivized purely through RL.

• A pipeline for DeepSeek-R1: two RL stages (find better reasoning patterns, align with human preferences) and two SFT stages (seed reasoning and non-reasoning skills).

• Reasoning patterns of a large model can be distilled into small ones — and that beats running RL on the small model directly.

• DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B: 55.5% on AIME 2024, beating QwQ-32B-Preview.

• DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B: 72.6% AIME 2024, 94.3% MATH-500, 57.2% LiveCodeBench — comparable to o1-mini.

• Open-sourced: 1.5B, 7B, 8B, 14B, 32B and 70B checkpoints (Qwen2.5 and Llama3).
Section 2.2.1 — Group Relative Policy Optimization (Shao et al., 2024)

elements.name: PPO — the usual RLHF setup (for comparison)

elements.text: The critic is typically as large as the policy — roughly double the memory and compute.

KL term goes straight
into the loss
no critic — the group mean is the baseline

J_GRPO(θ) = E[ q ~ P(Q),  {o₁ … o_G} ~ π_θold(O|q) ]
    (1/G) Σᵢ ( min( ρᵢ·Aᵢ ,  clip(ρᵢ, 1−ε, 1+ε)·Aᵢ )  −  β·D_KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref) )

    where  ρᵢ = π_θ(oᵢ|q) / π_θold(oᵢ|q)

D_KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref) = π_ref(oᵢ|q)/π_θ(oᵢ|q) − log( π_ref(oᵢ|q)/π_θ(oᵢ|q) ) − 1

Aᵢ = ( rᵢ − mean(r₁…r_G) ) / std(r₁…r_G)

ρᵢ — probability ratio
How much more (or less) likely the updated policy makes answer oᵢ than the policy that sampled it.

clip(…, 1−ε, 1+ε) and min
Caps how far one update can move: a pessimistic, trust-region-like step (from PPO).

β · D_KL
Keeps the policy close to the reference model. GRPO adds it to the loss, not to the reward.

Aᵢ — group-relative advantage
Answers better than their siblings’ average get pushed up; worse ones get pushed down. No critic needed.
Worked example — one question, G = 4 samples
Illustrative numbers (not from the paper): reward 1 = correct, 0 = wrong; std is the population std.

mean = 0.25   std ≈ 0.433

The one correct answer gets a large positive advantage (+1.73); the three wrong ones are mildly penalised (−0.58 each). If every sample were right — or every sample wrong — all advantages would be 0: nothing to learn from that question.

Why it matters here
Cheaper RL at scale: one fewer giant model in memory, and the baseline comes for free from sampling several answers per question.

The training loop (repeated for thousands of steps)
rule-based rewards — no neural reward model

Accuracy reward
Is the response correct? For math with a deterministic answer, the model must give its final answer in a set format (e.g. inside a box), so a rule can check it. For LeetCode-style problems, a compiler runs predefined test cases.

Format reward
The model must put its thinking process between ‘<think>’ and ‘</think>’ tags.

Why no neural reward model (outcome or process)?
• it can be reward-hacked in large-scale RL
• retraining it costs extra resources
• it complicates the whole pipeline

Section 2.2.4 — performance, self-evolution and the “aha moment”
Figure 2 — AIME accuracy of R1-Zero during training (16 samples per question)
Codeforces rating: o1-mini 1820 · o1-0912 1843 · R1-Zero 1444. Without a single supervised example, R1-Zero is competitive on math — and still behind on code.
Figure 3 — average response length on the training set during RL

Nobody told it to. As training goes on, R1-Zero spends more test-time compute — from hundreds to thousands of reasoning tokens per answer.

With that extra thinking, sophisticated behaviours appear spontaneously:

Q: If a > 1, the sum of the real solutions
   of √(a − √(a + x)) = x equals ?

<think> Square both sides …
  a − √(a + x) = x²
  (a − x²)² = a + x
  x⁴ − 2ax² − x + (a² − a) = 0
  …
  Wait, wait. Wait. That’s an aha moment
  I can flag here.
  Let’s reevaluate this step-by-step …
It learns to re-think, in an anthropomorphic tone — an aha moment for the researchers too.

The catch — drawbacks of R1-Zero
• poor readability: responses may lack markdown and are hard to follow
• language mixing: the chain of thought switches languages mid-way

From the stage-2 checkpoint: sample several answers per prompt, keep only the correct ones

Reasoning: some prompts are judged by DeepSeek-V3 as a generative reward model (ground truth + prediction). CoTs with mixed languages, long paragraphs or code blocks are filtered out.

MMLU · MMLU-Redux · MMLU-Pro · DROP · IF-Eval · GPQA Diamond · SimpleQA · FRAMES

Open-ended (LLM judge)
AlpacaEval 2.0 · Arena-Hard — GPT-4-Turbo-1106 judges pairwise; only the final summary is shown, to avoid length bias

Code
LiveCodeBench (Aug 2024 – Jan 2025) · Codeforces (10 Div.2 contests) · SWE-Bench Verified (agentless) · Aider-Polyglot (diff format)

Math
AIME 2024 · MATH-500 · CNMO 2024 (Chinese Math Olympiad)
Baselines: DeepSeek-V3, Claude-3.5-Sonnet-1022, GPT-4o-0513, OpenAI-o1-mini, OpenAI-o1-1217 (o1-1217 numbers come from official reports). Distilled models are also compared with QwQ-32B-Preview.
Why pass@k instead of greedy decoding?

Greedy decoding on long-output reasoning models gives more repetition and big swings between checkpoints. So every question is answered k times (k = 4 to 64 depending on test-set size) with temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.95, and generation is capped at 32,768 tokens.

pᵢ is 1 if the i-th response is correct, else 0 — pass@1 is the expected single-shot accuracy, with much lower variance than one greedy run.

cons@64 (used for AIME 2024) asks: if you sample 64 answers and pick the most common one, is it right? It shows what extra test-time compute buys.

Prompts: simple-evals for MMLU, DROP, GPQA, SimpleQA; Zero-Eval for MMLU-Redux; few-shot prompts converted to zero-shot for MMLU-Pro, C-Eval and CLUE-WSC — few-shot CoT can hurt R1.

Math ≈ o1-1217, far above the rest.
Knowledge (MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GPQA) beats V3 — gains come mostly from STEM questions, thanks to large-scale RL.
IF-Eval and AlpacaEval / ArenaHard jump: instruction-following data in the final SFT + RL stages helps writing and open QA.
Summaries stay short — 689 tokens on ArenaHard, 2,218 characters on AlpacaEval — so no length bias with GPT judges.
C-SimpleQA is worse than V3: after safety RL, R1 refuses some queries. Without safety RL it would score over 70%.
Engineering code: o1-1217 wins on Aider, ties on SWE Verified. RL data for this was still very limited.
8 · Distillation — teaching small models to reason
Llama-3.3 was picked over 3.1 because its reasoning is slightly better.

Deliberately simple: plain supervised fine-tuning on R1’s outputs. Adding RL would boost these models further, but the goal was to show how effective distillation alone is — the RL stage is left to the community.
32B and 70B beat o1-mini on most benchmarks
even 1.5B beats GPT-4o and Claude-3.5 on math (28.9% AIME, 83.9% MATH)
Other columns in Table 5 (GPQA, LiveCodeBench, Codeforces rating) show the same ordering; e.g. Distill-Qwen-32B: 62.1 GPQA, 57.2 LCB, 1691 rating.
§4.1 — Could the small model just do RL itself?
Conclusion 1 — distilling a stronger model into a small one works great; RL on the small model needs enormous compute and may still fall short of distillation.
Conclusion 2 — distillation is economical and effective, but pushing past the frontier of intelligence may still need more powerful base models and larger-scale RL.
Shared for insight — the authors stress this does not mean these approaches can never produce good reasoning models.
① What counts as a “step”? A fine-grained step is hard to define for general reasoning.
② Is this step correct? Auto-annotation by models is unreliable; manual labels don’t scale.
③ A model-based PRM invites reward hacking — and retraining it costs resources and complicates the pipeline.
Verdict: good for reranking top-N responses or guiding search — but its benefit is limited relative to the extra compute it adds in large-scale RL.

model emits tags for
reasoning steps

MCTS guided by a
pre-trained value model

chess: small, well-
defined search tree
① Token generation has an exponentially larger search space than chess. Capping each node’s expansion leads to local optima.
② The value model steers every step, but a fine-grained value model is hard to train — so iterative self-improvement stalls.

Verdict: MCTS helps at inference with a pre-trained value model, but boosting the model iteratively through self-search remains a major challenge. AlphaGo’s recipe doesn’t transfer easily to token generation.
Section 5 — conclusion, limitations and future work

R1-Zero shows pure RL can teach reasoning; R1, with cold-start data and iterative RL fine-tuning, reaches OpenAI-o1-1217 level; and distillation brings that reasoning to small dense models. The authors list four open problems:

General capability

Behind DeepSeek-V3 at function calling, multi-turn, complex role-playing and JSON output.
Next: use long CoT to improve these.

Language mixing

Optimized for Chinese and English — for other languages it may reason and answer in English.
Next: fix in future updates.

Prompt sensitivity

Few-shot prompting consistently hurts R1.
Advice: describe the problem directly and specify the output format, zero-shot.

Software engineering

Long evaluation times slow RL, so little RL was done here — small gains over V3.
Next: rejection sampling on SE data, asynchronous evaluation.
Give a strong base model verifiable rewards and room to think, and reasoning emerges — then make it readable, align it, and distil it.

§4.1 — Could the small model just do RL itself?
Conclusion 1 — distilling a stronger model into a small one works great; RL on the small model needs enormous compute and may still fall short of distillation.
Conclusion 2 — distillation is economical and effective, but pushing past the frontier of intelligence may still need more powerful base models and larger-scale RL.
Shared for insight — the authors stress this does not mean these approaches can never produce good reasoning models.
① What counts as a “step”? A fine-grained step is hard to define for general reasoning.
② Is this step correct? Auto-annotation by models is unreliable; manual labels don’t scale.
③ A model-based PRM invites reward hacking — and retraining it costs resources and complicates the pipeline.
Verdict: good for reranking top-N responses or guiding search — but its benefit is limited relative to the extra compute it adds in large-scale RL.

① Token generation has an exponentially larger search space than chess. Capping each node’s expansion leads to local optima.

Verdict: MCTS helps at inference with a pre-trained value model, but boosting the model iteratively through self-search remains a major challenge. AlphaGo’s recipe doesn’t transfer easily to token generation.
Section 5 — conclusion, limitations and future work

R1-Zero shows pure RL can teach reasoning; R1, with cold-start data and iterative RL fine-tuning, reaches OpenAI-o1-1217 level; and distillation brings that reasoning to small dense models. The authors list four open problems:

General capability

Behind DeepSeek-V3 at function calling, multi-turn, complex role-playing and JSON output.
Next: use long CoT to improve these.

Language mixing

Optimized for Chinese and English — for other languages it may reason and answer in English.
Next: fix in future updates.

Prompt sensitivity

Few-shot prompting consistently hurts R1.
Advice: describe the problem directly and specify the output format, zero-shot.

Software engineering

Long evaluation times slow RL, so little RL was done here — small gains over V3.
Next: rejection sampling on SE data, asynchronous evaluation.
Give a strong base model verifiable rewards and room to think, and reasoning emerges — then make it readable, align it, and distil it.
